title: The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equation (4) writes z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)), defining the redshift z as equal to the relativistic Doppler factor. However, the standard definition of cosmological redshift is z = (λ_obs - λ_emit)/λ_emit, making 1+z = λ_obs/λ_emit = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)). The derivation of Equation (5) — β = ((1+z)²-1)/((1+z)²+1) — is algebraically consistent only when 1+z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)), not when z equals that factor. The subsequent derivation consistently uses (1+z) as the Doppler factor throughout the paper, suggesting Equation (4) as printed contains a typographical omission of '1+' before z. Under lenient strictness this is treated as a presentation ambiguity rather than a substantive error, as the rest of the derivation is internally consistent when interpreted with the standard Doppler relation.

The paragraph beginning 'We can analyze the effect of aberration as seen in an inertial reference frame with a null relative velocity respect to us, very close to the CO, in a condition of motion relative to it; let's call it auxiliary reference frame. We suppose that the auxiliary reference frame is so close to the CO that the effects of general relativity are negligible as the Equivalence Principle states. Clearly this third reference frame will be inertial with both the other two. This enables us to describe the variation of the initial directions of photons as the usual special relativistic aberration. Then we will move from this auxiliary reference system to our actual position in an FLRW Universe, but not the reference frame.' appears twice in the paper in near-identical form — once at lines 49-51 and again at lines 53-55. This appears to be a copy-paste duplication artifact from the drafting process. It does not affect the scientific content but indicates an editorial oversight.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3 (first subsection), reference to neutron star mass limit
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper refers to the 'Volkov-Oppenheimer limit' regarding the maximum mass of neutron stars. The correct name for this limit is the 'Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit' (TOV limit). The names 'Volkoff' and 'Tolman' are misspelled/missing. This is a minor nomenclature error and does not affect any scientific arguments or conclusions in the paper.

summary: Verification of 'The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances' under exhaustive mode and lenient strictness found 3 minor issues, none of which reach high confidence or constitute a result-invalidating error. (1) Equation (4) contains an ambiguous definition: it writes z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)) where the standard Doppler relation gives 1+z = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)). The rest of the derivation (Eq. 5 onwards) consistently uses (1+z) as the Doppler factor, indicating this is a presentation typo. (2) A paragraph describing the auxiliary reference frame appears twice in near-identical form (lines 49-51 and 53-55), suggesting a copy-paste duplication. (3) The 'Volkov-Oppenheimer limit' should correctly be the 'Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff' (TOV) limit. The paper's central mathematical derivation — from relativistic aberration to the modified luminosity distance d_L = R³(t₀)/R²(t₁) r₁ with an extra (1+z) factor compared to the canonical formula — is internally consistent and algebraically sound. The Eq. (36) Hubble function is algebraically equivalent to the standard E²(z) parametrization from Carroll et al. 1992. The Etherington relation is preserved under the modified definitions. The paper is primarily a theoretical proposal with qualitative discussion of cosmological implications; it does not present numerical data or statistical analyses that can be independently verified. The three flagged issues are editorial in nature and do not undermine the paper's central arguments. No fabricated citations, cross-section contradictions, or figure inconsistencies were detected. Under lenient strictness, the paper passes verification.
